one: The overview course for AI: search, MDPs, graphical models, logic, and machine learning under one frame — making good decisions with incomplete information and limited compute.
pos: CS 221 is the entry point to Stanford's AI track, and the best way to see that AI is more than model tuning. It uses one mathematical language (probability + algorithms) to describe how agents make decisions with incomplete information and limited computation, spanning classical symbolic AI through modern machine learning.
topics: **Search and constraint satisfaction**: DFS/BFS/A*, heuristics, CSPs, local search
**Games and adversarial search**: minimax, alpha-beta, expected utility
**MDPs and reinforcement learning**: value iteration, policy iteration, Q-learning basics
**Probabilistic graphical models**: Bayesian networks, HMMs, variable elimination, sampling
**Machine learning**: naive Bayes, perceptron, logistic regression, losses and regularization
**Logic and knowledge representation**: propositional logic, first-order logic, inference
**Capstone project**: combine the modules into a working AI system
prereq: CS 103 (or 103B/X), CS 106B (or 106X), CS 109, and CS 161. The course explicitly says it will not reteach these foundations.
assess: Typically about five written/programming assignments plus a midterm, a final, and a capstone project; the workload is on the heavy side for a Stanford course. Check the current syllabus for exact weights.
who: Undergrads or students switching majors who want a complete AI map; anyone planning to take CS 229/224N/234 next; engineers who want to fill the classical-AI gap.
tips: Brush up on probability (CS 109) and algorithms (CS 161) first, or the assignments will hurt. Write the search and MDP parts from scratch rather than only calling libraries.
